items.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023
items.q: when I was on Woody Herman’s band playing with Ronnie and Sal Nistico and Frank Vicari, man that was a delight.

ctx.x: Well it helps not to be a prick. You know the more prickly your personality is the better you better be as a player to maintain a successful career. Because you know Gadd and I talk about this a lot. One thing about all these guys that I’ve spent my life playing with, and still play with, is they’ve never lost the magic of music, the feeling of delight and the exploration and trying to get better. Everybody that I know that is in my cohort is still striving. And so if you’re on time, if you have a pleasant…

yesterday. I’ve had experiences where, you know for me when I walk into a room and there’s other musicians playing I’m gravitating toward a center of pitch and an agreed upon place where we’re going to play, matching timbres, playing together. But there are some guys that you realize that they are by themselves. They are not listening to anybody else, and they don’t bend. So if you’re going to play with them you do the bending. But for instance like Alan Rubin, my colleague in the Blues Brothers Band and for so…

And there’s this myth I think that the fourth tenor and the second alto parts are easier. And often times they’re not because you get those, you fill in the harmonies and sometimes they’re a challenge to play and also you’re trying to fit in in the ensemble.
